newsitem.title: FRANCE: OECD sees Japan economy growing 2.9 pct in 1998.
newsitem.headline: OECD sees Japan economy growing 2.9 pct in 1998.

text.p: Japan's economic growth is expected to climb to 2.9 percent in calendar 1998, after slowing to an estimated 2.3 percent in 1997 from a robust 3.6 percent in 1996, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) said on Friday.
The Paris-based OECD said in its twice-yearly report that Japan's gross domestic product (GDP) is likely to mark a 2.9 percent rise in real terms in 1998, based on rising domestic demand.
The prediction is based on the assumption that the current fiscal tightening will be relaxed and that the current easy monetary policy stance will be maintained.
However, the OECD projection could be off target because of the possible appreciation of the yen, the report said.
OECD chief economist Stephen Potter told a news conference on Thursday that Japan's growth forecast was based on an exchange rate of 127 yen per dollar.
The OECD said a 10 percent appreciation of the yen would weaken the Japanese economic recovery by slashing GDP growth by 0.2 percentage point in 1997 and 0.8 percentage point in 1998.
On the other hand, a 10 percent yen rise would reduce inflation by 0.2 percentage point in 1997 and 0.5 percentage point in 1998, it said.

The initial impact from an appreciation of the yen on the current account surplus would be small, the report said, but over the 2000-2002 period, it would reduce the current account surplus by almost one percentage point of GDP, or nearly $40 billion.

In the first half of 1997, the recovery in output seemed to be continuing. Industrial production rose briskly in the first quarter, bringing the year-on-year increase to over 6.5 percent, the OECD report said.
This, in part, reflected temporary factors such as stable inventories and a boost in private consumption stemming from spending in advance of the April 1 rise in the sales tax.
In addition, business investment should continue to expand rapidly, and increased exports could raise the current account surplus to 1.8 percent of GDP.
However, the GDP growth may be held back during the middle quarters of 1997 as the second phase of the fiscal tightening reduces real personal disposable income.
